reviews.measuring-an-economy: This chapter built a toolkit for measuring an economy, and the distinction between stocks and flows runs through all of it. GDP measures a flow of output, while capital, wealth and natural capital are stocks that investment builds up and depreciation runs down. Price indexes such as the CPI and the GDP deflator separate real change from mere price change, though no index is ever perfect. Governments and central banks lean on these numbers when they steer the economy with fiscal and monetary policy. Yet GDP leaves out unpaid work, inequality and the environment's role as source and sink, which is why green national accounting and SNA 2025 try to count nature in.

nature-econ-505.title: The circular flow ignores the energy that drives it
nature-econ-505.text: The textbook circular flow has a hidden assumption. It implies the economy runs like a perpetual motion machine, something the {{ref:nature-eecon-118}} rule out. No economy can recycle its own waste without new energy, so it must operate as a subsystem of a larger ecosystem. In this critique, the economy depends on a one-way {{ref:nature-eecon-136}} of matter and energy from the environment. Concentrated, useful matter and energy enter from natural capital such as solar energy, oil wells, fisheries and mines. They leave as dispersed, useless waste, a change physicists describe with {{ref:nature-eecon-109}}. Because these inputs and the capacity to absorb waste are finite, there is a sustainable limit to the economy's growth. {{ref:nature-eecon-059}} therefore replaces the simple circular flow with a diagram that includes solar energy and the natural inputs and services it sustains.

nature-econ-501.title: Who owns the world's wealth
nature-econ-501.text: In 2013, 1% of adults were estimated to hold 46% of the world's wealth. In 2008 the estimate had been 40%, or 32% adjusted for purchasing power parity. The distribution of wealth describes how a society's or the world's total wealth is shared among people and regions. At the other end, some adults have negative net worth, with debts larger than their assets. The pattern described in {{ref:nature-eecon-164}} holds that inequality of wealth and income rises in early development, stabilizes, then falls.

nature-econ-482.title: Does inequality help or hurt growth?
nature-econ-482.text: Does inequality help an economy grow, or hold it back? Theories point in opposite directions. The classical view, from Adam Smith, held that inequality boosts saving by the wealthy and so speeds capital accumulation and growth. Galor and Zeira argued that where credit markets are imperfect, inequality harms investment in skills and slows growth, except in very poor economies. Galor and Moav suggest it helped early industrial growth but turned harmful once human capital replaced physical capital as the main engine. Thomas Piketty argued in 2013 that when the return on capital exceeds the growth rate of output, inequality rises.

nature-econ-540.title: Tobin's q: when buying new machines pays
nature-econ-540.text: Tobin's q compares two numbers: a physical asset's market value and the cost of replacing it. The ratio helps explain investment. When q is above 1, a machine can be bought for less than the output it generates is worth, so firms gain by investing.

nature-econ-493.title: Factor income: rent, wages, interest and profit
nature-econ-493.text: Each factor of production earns its own kind of income: rent from land, wages from labour, interest from capital and profit from enterprise. Together these make up factor income. National income is divided among the factors of production through the factor market. In consumer theory, income takes a narrower meaning: the budget a person can spend on different goods at their given prices.

nature-econ-530.title: Gross national income: counting by ownership, not location
nature-econ-530.text: Gross national income, formerly called gross national product or GNP, is the total factor income earned by a country's residents. It equals GDP plus factor income residents receive from abroad, minus factor income paid to non-residents. GDP defines its scope by location, GNI by ownership. For the whole world the two are the same. GNI is a concept of income rather than of {{ref:nature-econ-602}}. It includes the wages of cross-border and seasonal workers abroad, but not the remittances they send home, which is why France's GNI exceeds its GDP. The 1993 revision of the System of National Accounts renamed GNP as GNI. The United States used GNP as its main measure until 1991, when it switched to GDP. Subtracting depreciation gives {{ref:nature-econ-571}}. The gap between the two measures can matter a great deal. Ireland's GDP became so distorted by multinational profit shifting that in 2017 its central bank adopted a modified GNI measure.

nature-econ-571.title: Net national income: allowing for wear and tear
nature-econ-571.text: Machines, buildings and roads wear out, and gross national income ignores that loss. Net national income subtracts it: it is gross national income minus depreciation. It covers the income of households, businesses and government. Put another way, it equals GDP plus net wages, salaries and property income from abroad, minus wear and tear of buildings, machinery, equipment and infrastructure. By the expenditure method, it is consumption plus investment plus government spending plus net exports, plus net foreign factor income, minus indirect taxes and depreciation of manufactured capital.

nature-econ-492.title: Haig–Simons income: consumption plus change in net worth
nature-econ-492.text: A widely used economic definition of income dates from 1938. Haig–Simons income is consumption plus the change in a person's net worth: what is consumed plus the change in the value of property held. Tax law usually counts less. Taxable income is typically lower, because unrealized gains, such as a rise in share prices, are economic income but not taxable income. A broader idea, full income, adds non-monetary consumption ability to money income. It cannot be observed, so economists must rely on money income.

nature-econ-568.title: The unpaid work the national accounts ignore
nature-econ-568.text: An Australian study put the value of unpaid work, such as household work, at about 50% of GDP. None of it appears in any category of the national accounts, or in GDP. Because GDP is tied to the national accounts, the omission may distort the picture they give. Unpaid housework falls outside the SNA production boundary, the line that decides what counts as production. Feminist economists such as Marilyn Waring and Nancy Folbre call the SNA biased for valuing no unpaid housework, even though GDP imputes a rent for owner-occupied homes. They say the omission hides how much market production depends on non-market labour. Statisticians, for their part, question whether valuing such work is feasible.

nature-econ-589.title: The marginal propensity to save
nature-econ-589.text: Of each extra unit of income, a household spends some and saves the rest. The share saved is the marginal propensity to save. The share of total income saved, by contrast, is the average propensity to save. The general level of interest rates directly affects the saving rate.

nature-econ-546.title: The multiplier: how spending ripples through an economy
nature-econ-546.text: A government pays for a bridge. The bridge adds its own value to output, and the workers who built it can then spend and invest more. This is the multiplier effect: a change in spending is magnified as it passes through the economy, moving total output by more than the original change. Such spending can help close an output gap, the shortfall of output below its potential. Keynes showed that the logic also runs in reverse. A small fall in consumption or investment can be magnified into declines across the economy.

nature-econ-525.title: Does fiscal stimulus work?
nature-econ-525.text: When a government spends more or cuts taxes in a slump, what actually happens? Keynesians argue that expansionary fiscal policy in recessions builds the base for growth and full employment, with the deficits repaid by the later expansion. The models give a more mixed picture. In {{ref:nature-econ-558}}, fiscal expansion raises the price level and real interest rates in the long run. The AD–AS model lets the price level vary, which makes it better for long-run analysis. Economists still debate how effective fiscal stimulus is.

nature-econ-588.title: Do interest rates keep saving and investment equal?
nature-econ-588.text: Classical economists believed saving and investment would always match. If saving rose, interest rates would fall, and cheaper funds would stimulate investment. Keynes disagreed. He argued that both are insensitive to interest rates, so saving could exceed investment for long periods, causing a general glut and recession. Savings withheld from investment cut total spending, incomes and jobs, which in turn reduces savings again. The two camps remain divided on whether interest rates keep saving and investment equal.

nature-econ-558.title: The IS–LM model: two markets in balance
nature-econ-558.text: John Hicks invented the IS–LM model in 1936. It finds the interest rates and output levels at which two markets are in balance at once. In the goods market, investment must balance saving, which gives the IS part of the name. In the money market, money supply must balance money demand, which gives the LM part. The model underpins the idea of aggregate demand, by asking how much is demanded at a given price level.

nature-econ-497.title: Gross or net, domestic or national: decoding the names
nature-econ-497.text: A French-owned cotton factory in Senegal counts in Senegal's domestic figures but in France's national figures. That example captures half of a naming scheme. 'Domestic' counts everything produced inside a country's borders, while 'national' counts everything produced by its nationals anywhere. The other half is gross versus net. 'Gross' means the total product, while 'net' subtracts the amount needed to offset depreciation of fixed capital. So net domestic product is GDP minus depreciation of capital. Each measure can also be framed as product, income or expenditure.

nature-econ-498.title: Is national income a good measure of welfare?
nature-econ-498.text: Cleaning up an oil spill adds to GDP, while the lost well-being from fouled beaches goes unmeasured. A paid nanny's income counts in GDP, but a parent's unpaid childcare does not. Such cases raise the question of how well GDP per person reflects people's welfare. It is not useless: countries with higher GDP may also score higher on other welfare measures, such as life expectancy. Still, alternatives exist, including indexes of human development, sustainable economic welfare and genuine progress, and a sustainable version of national income.

nature-econ-529.title: Two centuries of global income inequality
nature-econ-529.text: From 1820 to 2002, the global income Gini rose steadily, with a sharp increase between 1980 and 2002. That measure tracks income inequality among all the world's people, not just within single countries. The trend appears to have peaked and started to reverse, as emerging economies such as the BRIC countries grew rapidly.

nature-econ-528.title: Where the Gini coefficient falls short
nature-econ-528.text: The Gini coefficient is a relative measure, so it can rise even while the number of people in absolute poverty falls. That is one of several weaknesses. It is not additive, and different income distributions can share the same value. A population can have a very low income Gini and a very high wealth Gini at once. Small populations with less varied economies also tend to report lower values.

nature-econ-507.title: Weighting the CPI: why housing counts most
nature-econ-507.text: In one example of a consumer price index, housing carries 41.4% of the weight, food and beverages 17.4% and transport 17.0%. Each weight reflects that item's share of consumer spending, so a price change in housing moves the index more than the same change in a smaller category. Ideally the weights would reflect current spending, but in practice they use the most recent past data. Updating the weights only now and then saves money, but it delays new kinds of spending, such as Internet subscriptions, from entering the index.

nature-econ-572.title: Adjusted net national income: subtracting nature's losses
nature-econ-572.text: Net national income allows for machines wearing out, but not for minerals dug up and gone. Adjusted net national income makes that further correction, subtracting the running down of resources taken from nature. Economists divide capital into categories, among them manufactured capital and two kinds of natural capital. The non-critical kind includes minerals, and that is what gets deducted. The critical kind, such as air and water, is not accounted for; {{ref:nature-eecon-229}} returns to it. The European Environment Agency has proposed using the consumption of ecosystem capital to create an adjusted net national income.

nature-econ-503.title: From two sectors to five: building up the circular flow
nature-econ-503.text: The simplest circular flow has just two sectors: households and firms, with households spending all their income on firms' output. Each added sector brings the model closer to a real economy. The three-sector model adds government. The four-sector model adds foreign trade and capital flows. The five-sector model adds banks and other intermediaries, which borrow household savings and lend for firms' investment.

nature-econ-504.title: Leakages and injections: money leaving and entering the flow
nature-econ-504.text: Not all income flows straight back into spending. Saved money is a leakage: it is not spent, so not all output gets bought. Taxes are a leakage too, and imports a third. Injections add money back in: investment, government spending on services and welfare payments, and exports. In the five-sector model, the economy is in equilibrium when total leakages equal total injections. Savings plus taxes plus imports must equal investment plus government spending plus exports.

nature-econ-518.title: The capital consumption allowance: running to stand still
nature-econ-518.text: Part of every year's GDP buys no growth at all. It simply keeps the country's productive capacity from shrinking. This is the capital consumption allowance, the part of GDP due to depreciation. It covers wear and tear on physical capital, plus the investment needed to maintain human capital, such as educating workers to replace retirees. GDP equals net domestic product plus the capital consumption allowance.

nature-econ-573.title: Net national product: output after depreciation
nature-econ-573.text: Net national product is gross national product minus depreciation, the loss in value of fixed capital through wear and tear in production. Net domestic product is, likewise, GDP minus depreciation. Economics research usually uses the gross measures instead, a choice that has long been disputed. The net measures matter for the environment. Net national product serves as an indicator of sustainability in environmental economics and appears in models of resources running out. Research has also studied it as a dynamic welfare indicator.

nature-econ-602.title: Value added: what each producer contributes
nature-econ-602.text: A firm buys in materials and services, works on them, and sells the result. The difference between the market value of what it sells and the value of what it used is its value added. A firm's total value added equals its revenue minus {{ref:nature-econ-536}}, the inputs it uses up. It roughly equals pay to employees, a return to labour, plus earnings before taxes, a return to capital. In macroeconomics, value added is the contribution of capital and labour to a product's value, so national value added is shared between them. In national accounts, gross value added is gross output minus those used-up inputs, which equals net output. Net value added deducts depreciation from it. Add up gross value added across the whole economy at market prices and you get GDP.

nature-econ-536.title: Intermediate consumption: inputs used up in production
nature-econ-536.text: In the US economy, intermediate consumption is about 45% of gross output. It is the total value of goods and services that businesses use up as inputs while producing, such as raw materials, services and other running costs. Some inputs change form, like bulk sugar; others are used up completely, like electric power. It equals the gap between gross output, roughly total sales value, and net output, which is gross value added or GDP. Because it is subtracted from gross output to get GDP, how it is defined and estimated strongly affects the size of the GDP figure. Ordinary maintenance, repairs and research and development spending count as intermediate consumption. Depreciation of fixed assets and major renovations that extend an asset's life do not. Some odd results follow. Buying a service from another firm instead of doing it in-house raises a firm's intermediate consumption and lowers its own value added. And when businesses buy physical assets GDP rises, while renting or leasing them lowers GDP, because lease payments count as intermediate consumption.

nature-econ-484.title: Three ways to measure GDP
nature-econ-484.text: GDP can be measured three ways, and in theory all three give the same total. The production approach, the most direct, adds up the output of every class of enterprise. It is also called the value-added approach, because it counts how much value is contributed at each stage of production. The income approach sums the primary incomes paid out by producers; measured this way, the total is called {{ref:nature-econ-490}}. The expenditure approach adds up final uses of goods and services, leaving out intermediate consumption. Within each country, a national statistical agency normally does the measuring.

nature-econ-581.title: Labour productivity: output per hour of work
nature-econ-581.text: A country's ability to raise its living standards over time is said to depend almost entirely on raising output per worker. Labour productivity measures exactly that: output volume, such as GDP or gross value added, divided by labour input, such as total hours worked or total employment. Output is usually measured as value added, the value of outputs minus intermediate inputs, to avoid double counting. Total hours worked is generally preferred to a headcount, which can hide changes in average hours. Labour productivity is a key indicator of growth, competitiveness and living standards. Yet productivity and wages do not always move together. They can decouple.

nature-econ-490.title: Gross domestic income: GDP counted from the income side
nature-econ-490.text: Everything produced and sold generates an equal amount of income, so GDP can also be counted from the income side. Gross domestic income does exactly that, adding up the primary incomes paid out by producers in a country. It should give the same total as the expenditure method.

nature-econ-567.title: The linked accounts that make up a nation's books
nature-econ-567.text: A nation's accounts are not one ledger but a linked set: production, income, expenditure, capital and financial accounts, plus balance sheets. Each account has a balancing item. These include value added, which equals GDP for the whole economy, along with disposable income, saving, net lending or borrowing, and net worth. Balance sheets record the stock of financial and non-financial assets and liabilities at a point in time. Accounts can be shown gross or net of consumption of fixed capital, the national-accounts version of depreciation.

nature-econ-496.title: Avoiding double counting: the meat that is counted once
nature-econ-496.text: Meat is worth $10 at the farm, $30 at the butcher and $60 at the supermarket. Adding the three sales gives $100, but only $60 enters national output. The rule is to count only the final value of a good, or the value added at each stage, not every sale along the chain. Here the values added are $10, $20 and $30, which sum to the same final value. In general, GDP at market price equals the value of output minus intermediate consumption.

nature-econ-603.title: Value-added tax: taxing each stage of production
nature-econ-603.text: A value-added tax is a tax on sales that is charged at each stage of production, but only on the value that stage adds. It is assessed step by step on a product or service, so each stage is taxed on its own unit value added.

nature-econ-537.title: Imputed rent: the rent homeowners pay themselves
nature-econ-537.text: Homeowners who live in their own houses pay no rent, yet national accounts record one for them. The imputed rent of owner-occupied housing is the market rent owner-occupiers would receive if they rented their homes out, and it is added to value added and so to GDP. The idea is that a dwelling provides its owner with a service, whether or not anyone pays for it. Critics call this addition largely fictitious, since nearly all owner-occupiers do not actually rent out their homes.

nature-econ-508.title: Owner-occupied housing: the CPI's long-running puzzle
nature-econ-508.text: What does it cost to live in a home you own? Statisticians and economists have long disagreed over how a consumer price index should count it. Many economists argue the index should include the opportunity cost of living in one's own home. A spending approach would count repairs, maintenance and also mortgage interest. A transaction-price approach would count only purchases of new dwellings, treating them like other durable goods. No single method has won agreement.
